title: Industry Structure, Competitive Moat & External Learning Hub

epigraph.quote: A truly great business must have an enduring moat that protects excellent returns on invested capital.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, 2007

web_blocks.text: A moat is whatever stops a rival from taking your profit. Greaves competes in four unrelated industries, so it has four moat questions: gensets, three-wheeler and OEM engines, industrial engines, and electric two- and three-wheelers. The evidence is thinner than we would like, because the filings name few customers or competitors and publish no engine market shares [6]. We use the operating data available from Greaves and its peers, and flag each gap.

web_blocks.caption: Operating comparison with listed peers, Q2 FY27 (quarter to September 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Every B2B engine and genset peer lost margin to commodity inflation while revenue grew. Greaves’ core margin of 11.5% sits close to Kirloskar’s standalone 11.0%, so the compression is an industry cycle, not a Greaves failure [1][81]. It also shows little short-run pricing power: when costs rise, the same four-to-five-month lag hits everyone. The EV peer is different: Ather’s positive EBITDA is only its second such quarter, on 93,211 units against about 37,649 billed by GEML [80][1].

web_blocks.text: Gensets are the segment where scale and service decide. Mahindra Powerol was number one in FY25 with 23.8% of 1,51,634 diesel gensets, and the top five (Cummins India, Kirloskar, Caterpillar, Mahindra Powerol and Greaves) account for roughly 55–60% of organised revenue [79][90][88]. Greaves’ own share is about 4% [30][29]. The CPCB IV+ emission rule (a pollution standard for diesel gensets up to 800 kW, effective July 2023) added exhaust after-treatment and electronic injection, prices rose 5–18% and volumes ran at 80–85% of the earlier CPCB-II level [88][89][90][91]. That favours engineering depth. Greaves has a complete 160–750 kVA range, remote monitoring and a service network [1]. It lacks an in-house very-high-horsepower engine, which it buys from a partner, and its data-centre play is “limited” in the CEO’s word [62]. Our view is that buyers weigh service and brand above the engine, so this moat is modest and rests on dealer quality.

Three-wheeler diesel engines are the strongest moat and the weakest market. Greaves calls itself the largest maker of single-cylinder diesel engines, with about 60% of diesel three-wheeler engines on VAHAN data, and it is sole engine supplier to a French microcar maker [44][6][62]. Qualification and multi-year contracts protect that share. But India Ratings writes that “the 3W diesel engine industry is continuously shrinking amid rising environmental concerns, although GCL remains a market leader” [70]. These engines were ₹545 crore, or 15.8% of group revenue, in FY26 and about 42% of Mobility Solutions in H1 FY27 [3][1]. The L5 industry (auto-rickshaw-type three-wheelers) sold about 8 lakh units in FY26, with an electric share near 33% against 23% a year earlier [6]. Management concedes that the move to CNG and electric is “more gradual than we expected” [27]. The moat is real, and so is the erosion of the ground it defends.

Excel and Industrial Solutions are narrower. Excel defends itself with customisation and certification (IATF, ISO, CE) at OEMs; the filings name no competitors, so we cannot rank it [6]. Industrial Solutions has a harder moat in firefighting, where FM/UL listing, which “very few companies in the world” hold, gates global fire-pump OEMs [62][1]. In farm equipment there was no moat: Chinese imports made finished machines uncompetitive and Greaves exited [62].

web_blocks.caption: Electric two-wheeler registrations, October 2026 and January–October 2026
web_blocks.takeaway: In October 2026 TVS, Bajaj and Hero together held 62.3% against 53.0% a year earlier and took about 81% of incremental volume, while Ola was the only top-ten decliner [84][86][85]. Ampere is sixth, and its 10,838 registrations rose 40%, slower than the 48% growth of the whole market. Trackers differ by a few hundred vehicles because VAHAN records late registrations. The pattern says buyers choose on brand reach, finance and price, with low switching cost once a customer rides another make. Share gains by incumbents show what the moat in this segment actually is: dealer density, service and cost of capital.

web_blocks.text: Policy shapes the e-2W market more than any moat. PM E-DRIVE (the ministry’s EV scheme, notified 29 September 2024) now has an outlay of ₹11,900 crore, raised from ₹10,900 crore on 10 August 2026, and runs to 31 March 2028. The e-2W incentive was ₹5,000 per kWh capped at ₹10,000 in FY25 and is now ₹2,500 per kWh capped at ₹5,000, for vehicles under ₹1.5 lakh ex-factory. The L5 e-3W incentive closed on 26 December 2025 when funds ran out [75][76][77]. Cutting GST on petrol two-wheelers and ICE three-wheelers from 28% to 18% narrowed the electric price advantage [6]. A subsidy available to every maker is not a moat. It is a hazard, and GEML already lost ₹477.32 crore to a subsidy dispute [8].

web_blocks.takeaway: Greaves owns narrow moats in the businesses that earn the margin and none in the one that burns cash. The core rests on qualification and an installed base, which erode slowly but sit in flat or shrinking markets. The EV franchise rests on a dealer base of 418 that is still being built and on subsidies anyone can claim. Pricing power shows up only with a lag: core raw-material cost rose from 63.9% to 67.8% of sales in a year [1].

web_blocks.title: The bull case, steelmanned
paragraphs: Greaves has real positions: about 60% of diesel three-wheeler engines, a sole-supplier relationship in Europe, a complete medium-horsepower genset range and a spares network that reaches 7,000 retailers [6][62][1]. Core revenue grew 24% in Q2 FY27, gensets 36% and auto engines 37%, and the margin dip matches peers while contracts are indexed to catch up from Q4 FY27 [1][62]. In EVs, loss per unit fell from ₹20,000 to ₹6,300 in a year on a plant at about 40% of its design, so the gain from spreading fixed cost is largely unspent [1]. The core holds ₹110 crore of net cash, the rating is AA-, no promoter shares are pledged, and ₹530 crore of fresh equity funds GEML for 12–18 months [62][69][67].

web_blocks.title: The bear case, steelmanned
paragraphs: The core product is exposed to a declining engine type, and India Ratings says so [70]. Core EBITDA margin fell 290 basis points in a year while revenue rose 20%, and management admits recovery has been “slower than we had anticipated” [1][62]. GEML has never been profitable, has raised equity three times in four years (₹1,171 crore in 2022, ₹29.5 crore from minority holders in FY25 and ₹530 crore in 2026), and faces incumbents that took 81% of new volume [9][2][84]. Write-offs recur: ₹477.32 crore in FY24, ₹39.34 crore in FY26 and ₹60.1 crore in Q2 FY27, even after a statement of “nothing more at this stage” [8][6][2][62]. Group operating cash flow was negative in FY22–FY25 and in H1 FY27 [6][2]. The ₹15,000 crore FY30 ambition needs roughly 44% annual growth (derived) against a 16–20% organic target [28][6].

web_blocks.text: Our independent judgment is that both cases are partly right because they describe different businesses. The core is a good, narrow-moat industrial franchise in modest-growth markets, and its margin dip looks cyclical: Kirloskar fell by a similar three points and Greaves’ contracts index with a lag [1][81][62]. We put the probability at roughly 60% that core EBITDA margin returns to at least 13%, the floor of management’s range, within about four quarters after pass-through completes, about 25% that it settles between 11% and 13%, and about 15% that it stays below 11% because metals keep rising or rivals discount. GEML has no moat today, a halved subsidy and strong incumbents. We think sustained positive EBITDA by the end of FY28 is below even, near 40%, because unit loss is falling fast yet volume must keep scaling while incumbents defend share. The core argument rests on pass-through, and the EV argument rests on cash.

web_blocks.mechanism: One of India’s earliest electric scooter makers was an early FAME subsidy beneficiary with a low-speed portfolio and a large dealer network [92]. It was named among makers accused of breaking the Phased Manufacturing Programme (local-sourcing) rules, and the ministry sought about ₹133 crore back, which Hero disputed while claiming ₹556 crore of unpaid subsidy. Buyers moved to faster scooters from Ola, Ather and TVS, working capital tightened and new products came late. A government committee first found no violation, but an independent fraud investigation continued.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Insolvency began on 20 December 2024. The highest-voted rescue plan won 47.66% of creditor votes against the 66% required, the process expired on 13 February 2026, and the tribunal ordered liquidation in March 2026. Admitted claims included Bank of Baroda ₹55.36 crore, South Indian Bank ₹17.62 crore, IDFC First Bank ₹9.43 crore and an unsecured vendor ₹47.87 crore [92].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: GEML shares the exposure: a FAME refund of ₹139.98 crore, a low-speed Reo line, and a net worth of only ₹59.65 crore at 31 March 2026 before the 2026 rights issue [8][6]. It differs in having a parent that put in ₹331.12 crore and a rated balance sheet [2][72]. One failure is not a statistic, but the mechanism is clear, and Cummins’ electrolyzer write-down below shows the same pattern in a stronger company. Subsidy dependence without scale is where the risk concentrates, so share (4.8%) and unit loss (−₹6,300) matter more than any single quarter.

web_blocks.text: A second data point comes from a legacy engine maker. Cummins booked a $240 million non-cash charge in the quarter ended September 2025 and began a strategic review of its electrolyzer business after sales fell well short of a $400 million target set in 2020 [93]. A very good engine franchise took large write-downs when a new market lacked policy-backed demand, which is why our scorecard treats the EV moat as unproven.

book_paragraphs: Suppose you and I owned a corner shop. What would stop a rival from opening next door and taking half our customers? Answer that, and you have found the moat. Warren Buffett built a career on that question, and it is the right one to ask of Greaves. But Greaves is not a corner shop. It sells engines to vehicle makers, gensets to hospitals, spares to mechanics and scooters to families. Each of those is a different shop with a different street, and each deserves its own answer.

Take the engines first, because they are the oldest part of the company. Greaves says it is the largest maker of single-cylinder diesel engines in the country and holds about 60% of diesel three-wheeler engines. A vehicle maker will not change that supplier lightly, because the engine has to pass emission tests and years of durability checks. A French microcar maker uses a Greaves engine and has no second source. That is a real moat. Now the other side of the ledger: the credit-rating agency writes that the three-wheeler diesel engine industry is “continuously shrinking”, although Greaves remains its leader. A strong castle on a shrinking island is still a strong castle, but the island is getting smaller.

Gensets are a different contest. Picture a hospital manager choosing a standby generator. She cares about three things: will it start, will someone come when it does not, and what will the spares cost? The engine inside matters less to her than the service van. Mahindra Powerol sold about 24% of the country’s diesel gensets in FY25. Greaves has about 4%, by its own estimate. The company’s medium-horsepower range grew 35% in the first half of the year, and that is good news, but the CEO is honest about the limits: “We do high horsepower engines but at a limited level.” Data centres want exactly that kind of engine.

Look at the numbers for the quarter to September 2026. Greaves’ core margin was 11.5%, down from 14.8%. Kirloskar Oil Engines, a peer that makes similar products, went from 14.0% to 11.0%. Cummins India saw profit before tax fall 28% on only 4% higher sales. Costs rose for everyone, and no one could pass them on at once. What does that tell you? That the squeeze is a cycle, and that none of these companies has the kind of pricing power that lets a business raise prices on the day its costs rise.

Think about switching costs for a moment, because they are the heart of any moat. When a vehicle maker changes its engine, it must retest the vehicle, retrain its line and risk a recall. That is costly, so engine suppliers keep customers for years. When a hospital changes its genset brand, it risks nothing but a phone call to a new dealer. So the same company enjoys sticky customers in one business and fickle ones in another. Qualification cycles, the months or years a part needs to be approved, protect the first and barely touch the second. Before you trust any claim of a moat, ask how long it would take a rival to be approved, and what the customer would lose by waiting.

Then there is the electric scooter, where the picture changes sharply. In October 2026, Indian buyers registered about 2.24 lakh electric two-wheelers. TVS took 27%, Bajaj 22%, Ather 14%, Hero 13%, and Ampere about 4.8%. The three biggest legacy two-wheeler makers lifted their combined share from 53% to 62% in a year and captured about four out of every five extra vehicles. Why? Because they already had showrooms, service centres, parts and low-cost loans. In this market, your moat is a dealer on every corner and a mechanic who knows the bike. A newcomer, even a well-funded one, has to build those before it can earn a margin.

What does Ampere have to set against that? A value price, a captive lender that approves a loan in under 2.5 minutes, batteries that all use the LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry, and a motor without rare-earth magnets that is due in new launches from the fourth quarter of FY27. These are useful edges, and the unit loss shows they are working: from ₹20,000 a scooter to ₹6,300 in a year. But they are edges, not walls. A rival can copy a loan product in a quarter, and a larger rival can fund price cuts for longer than a smaller one can fund losses.

Policy sits on top of all this. The government’s PM E-DRIVE scheme pays up to ₹5,000 on each eligible electric two-wheeler, half of the first-year cap, and the three-wheeler window closed in December 2025 when the money ran out. Every maker can claim it, so it is a tide, not a moat. Greaves learned the hard way what a tide can do: the ministry challenged its parts sourcing under the earlier scheme, and the company refunded ₹139.98 crore and provided for ₹337.34 crore more. A good rule is to ask, of any subsidised business, what its margin would be if the cheque stopped arriving.

The bull and the bear both have a case. The bull says Greaves has narrow but real moats in engines, a growing genset range, a spares network and a core that holds ₹110 crore of net cash. Its electric scooter loss per unit has fallen from ₹20,000 to ₹6,300 in a year on a plant that is only 40% used. The bear answers that the core margin has fallen from 14.8% to 11.5% in a year, the electric arm has asked its owners for fresh equity twice since 2022, write-offs keep coming, and the ₹15,000 crore ambition for FY30 needs growth near 44% a year. Both have the facts right. They are describing two companies.

Our judgment follows that split. For the core, we think it is more likely than not, roughly six chances in ten, that the margin climbs back to at least 13% once metal costs have been passed on. For the electric arm, we think sustained positive EBITDA by the end of FY28 is a little less likely than not, near four in ten. These are our probabilities, not the company’s promises. We would change them if metal prices keep rising, if the subsidy is cut again, or if scooter volume stalls while the plant stays at 40% use.

History offers a warning. Hero Electric was one of India’s earliest electric scooter makers and an early recipient of subsidy. The ministry demanded about ₹133 crore back for alleged breaches of local-sourcing rules, buyers moved to faster scooters, and the company went into insolvency. Its best rescue plan won 47.66% of creditor votes when 66% was needed, and a tribunal ordered liquidation in March 2026. Greaves is not Hero Electric. It has a rated parent that has put in ₹331 crore, and a share near five percent, though it also sells a low-speed line. But the same two things threaten both: dependence on a subsidy and a shortage of scale.

Charlie Munger liked to say, “Invert, always invert.” Instead of asking how this company succeeds, ask what would have to go wrong for it to fail. For Greaves the list is short: metals keep climbing, the subsidy falls, scooter share stalls under five percent and the parent keeps funding. If you can watch those four things, you will know more about this company than most of the people who talk about it. The last section of the web edition lists where to watch, listen and read for yourself.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A moat is not a thing a company says about itself. It is a gap between what a rival would have to spend to copy you and what you earn by not being copied. Greaves has such a gap in three-wheeler engines and firefighting engines, a thin one in gensets and none yet in electric scooters. The investor’s task is to match each belief to evidence, and to remember that a subsidy, however welcome, is never a moat.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Failures teach more reliably than successes. Hero Electric did not fail because electric scooters were a bad idea. It failed because it depended on a subsidy it could not control, lost to better products and ran short of cash. When we weigh GEML, we are really asking how much of its progress depends on its parent’s balance sheet, and how much on its own customers.
